add_eyes.name: Michiel Adriaenszoon de Ruyter
add_eyes.role: Lieutenant-Admiral of Holland and West Friesland, 59, commander of the Dutch fleet in its flagship De Zeven Provinciën
add_eyes.where: Quarterdeck of De Zeven Provinciën, off the Flemish banks and the Thames estuary, 11–14 June 1666 N.S.
add_eyes.authenticity: De Ruyter kept a shipboard journal (daghregister/journaal) kept in New Style dates. Gerard Brandt drew on it heavily for his Leven en bedryf van den heere Michiel de Ruiter (1687). The entries here come from a modern secondary account that quotes it (De Ruyter Foundation's study of the 1666 battle). The journal itself was not read directly for this chapter.
add_eyes.bio: The Dutch commander-in-chief in the Four Days' Battle, the very fleet whose guns Evelyn heard from his garden. His journal is a working seaman's log, not a reflective diary. It records cables cut and anchors lost and a mainmast shot away, and it is notably silent on moments that later writers made dramatic.

sources.title: De Ruyter Foundation: 'Strateeg — zeeslagen 1666: Vierdaagse' (PDF, cites the journal)
Brandt, Leven en bedryf van den heere Michiel de Ruiter (DBNL)

add_eyes.name: Jodocus van Lodenstein
add_eyes.role: Dutch Reformed minister at Utrecht, a leading voice of the pietist 'Further Reformation', about 46
add_eyes.where: Utrecht, far inland, hearing the news of the fleet
add_eyes.authenticity: His hymn on the Four Days' Battle is printed in his collected Uytspanningen (many editions from 1676 on). DBNL's calendar dates it by its subject, the fight of 1–4 June 1666. Lodenstein dated his title by the Dutch Old-Style-looking day numbers 1–4 June, which is unusual because the Republic used New Style; this may follow the English reckoning or the edition's choice. The date and title are confirmed. The text was not read line by line, so the content is summarised only from its title and genre.
add_eyes.bio: A strict, inward-looking pietist minister who distrusted worldly triumph, yet he wrote a hymn of victory over the English. That makes him a Dutch counterpart to Josselin, the Essex vicar who prayed over the same battle from the other side.

sources.title: DBNL calendar, 2 June 1666 (lists 'Sege-Sang over d'overwinninge in 't gevegt tegen Engelse 1, 2, 3, 4 Juny 1666')

add_eyes.name: Jeremias de Decker
add_eyes.role: Amsterdam poet and merchant's clerk, in the last months of his life
add_eyes.where: Amsterdam, reading the news from London
add_eyes.authenticity: 'Op 't afgebrande Londen' was printed posthumously in his collected verse (Lof der geldsucht, ofte Vervolg der rym-oeffeningen, 1702 ed. on DBNL). De Decker died in Amsterdam late in 1666, so the poem must date from between the news of the Fire (mid-September 1666 N.S.) and his death. It is not otherwise dated.
add_eyes.bio: A gentle, devout Amsterdam poet best known for a satire on greed. His poem on the burning of London refuses to gloat. It reads the Fire as God's judgement but says Europe and the free Netherlands should mourn, and it turns the moral into a warning to sea-raiders, with Holmes's burning of the Vlie only weeks old.

add_eyes.name: C. Groenveld, Pieter IJsbrand van der Hof and C.G. Kleyn (Hoorn verse writers)
add_eyes.role: Amateur poets and playwrights of Hoorn, a merchant port on the Zuiderzee that sent shipping through the Vlie
add_eyes.where: Hoorn, about 60 km from the Vlie anchorage burned by Holmes
add_eyes.authenticity: Their piece 'De wet der vergeldingh in 't verbrande Londen, ten thoon gestelt op den 12, 13, 14 en 15 Sept. 1666' is printed in the collection Het nieuwe Hoornse speel-werck. DBNL's calendar files it under September 1666. The days in the title are the Fire's days in New Style. Only the title was confirmed; the text was not read. Treat it as public printed opinion, not private writing.
add_eyes.bio: Collective, public, and partisan. The title alone, 'The law of retribution in burned London', tells you how a port that had just lost ships at the Vlie wanted the Fire read. Set beside De Decker's refusal to gloat, it shows the Dutch were divided over how to take England's disaster.

sources.title: DBNL calendar, September 1666 (lists 'De wet der vergeldingh in 't verbrande Londen')

add_entries.date_display: Friday 11 June 1666 (N.S., the Dutch calendar) = 1 June 1666 O.S. in England
add_entries.place: De Zeven Provinciën, at anchor off the Flemish coast, then under way
add_entries.headline: Cables cut, anchors left behind as the fleet surges forward
add_entries.digest: Albemarle's English squadron comes down on the Dutch fleet at anchor. To get under way fast, many Dutch ships simply cut their anchor cables. De Ruyter has his people write down exactly how much cable and how many anchors are being lost, a bookkeeper's note in the middle of the opening of the longest sea battle of the age. To the English diarists this is 1 June. To De Ruyter's logbook it is the 11th.
add_entries.source_note: De Ruyter's journal as cited in the De Ruyter Foundation study of the Four Days' Battle (PDF, deruyter.org); journal not read directly

add_entries.place: De Zeven Provinciën, mid-Channel off the Flemish banks
add_entries.headline: Mainmast shot away at about three in the afternoon
add_entries.digest: On the second day the flagship is badly mauled. De Ruyter's journal notes that his mainmast was shot away, around three o'clock. It says nothing about handing over or sharing command at that moment, a silence that later historians have noticed. The terse entry contrasts with Evelyn, who on the same day could only hear the guns from his garden in Deptford.
add_entries.source_note: De Ruyter Foundation PDF (deruyter.org), footnote on the journal's entry for 12 June

add_entries.date_display: June 1666 (title dates the fight '1, 2, 3, 4 Juny 1666') — written after the battle ended on 14 June N.S.
add_entries.headline: A pietist minister sings a hymn of victory
add_entries.digest: News reaches Utrecht that the fleet has beaten the English over four days. Lodenstein, a pietist minister usually wary of worldly glory, writes a 'Sege-Sang' (victory song) on the fight of 1–4 June, giving thanks in the form of a sacred hymn. Across the North Sea, Josselin was praying over the same battle in Essex, and Evelyn was learning that the English 'victory' had been a narrow escape.
add_entries.source_note: Title and dating from DBNL calendarium (2 June 1666), Lodenstein, Uytspanningen; text not read line-by-line, so the content is summarised from title and genre

add_entries.date_display: September 1666 (N.S.); title dates the Fire to 12–15 Sept. 1666 N.S. = 2–5 Sept. O.S. in London
add_entries.headline: 'The law of retribution': a Dutch port reads London's fire
add_entries.digest: Barely six weeks after Holmes burned some 150 merchant ships in the Vlie, the nearest anchorage to Hoorn's own trade, a group of Hoorn verse writers presents the burning of London as the law of retribution at work. They date the disaster by the Dutch calendar, 12 to 15 September, ten days later than the dates Pepys and Evelyn wrote. This is public printed opinion and carries none of the private doubt of a diary.
add_entries.source_note: DBNL calendarium, September 1666: 'De wet der vergeldingh in 't verbrande Londen, ten thoon gestelt op den 12, 13, 14 en 15 Sept. 1666', in Het nieuwe Hoornse speel-werck; title only verified

add_entries.date_display: Between mid-September and November 1666 (N.S.) — undated poem, written before the poet's death late in 1666
add_entries.headline: Do not rejoice at a neighbour's ruin
add_entries.digest: De Decker heads his poem 'Urbs antiqua ruit' (the ancient city falls) and calls the Fire the vengeance of God on London's streets and riches. But he says Europe and the free Netherlands mourn it, and that it goes against nature to delight in a neighbour's ruin. He ends by warning the sea-robbers that fire can punish fire, so that whoever plunders by water may yet be eaten by flames. It is a pointed glance at the English raid on the Vlie.
add_entries.source_note: De Decker, 'Op 't afgebrande Londen', Lof der geldsucht, ofte Vervolg der rym-oeffeningen (1702 ed.), DBNL deck001lofd02_01_0082; dating inferred from the event and his death in 1666

add_convergences.label: Autumn 1666: Dutch and continental verdicts on the burned city
add_convergences.note: Hoorn, which had just lost ships at the Vlie, calls the Fire retribution. Amsterdam's De Decker sees judgement but forbids gloating. In Paris, Giustinian hears Louis XIV call it a stroke of luck and then pairs the Vlie and London as twin disasters. All three date the Fire 12–15 September, while London's own diarists write 2–5 September.

add_ties.note: Van de Velde the Elder sailed in a galliot with De Ruyter's fleet in June 1666 and drew the council of war aboard De Zeven Provinciën.
On 11–12 June 1666 N.S. De Ruyter was fighting the battle whose guns Evelyn heard from his garden at Sayes Court.
Two country clergymen on opposite shores turned the same four-day battle into prayer: one gave thanks for victory, the other begged deliverance.
Both Dutch, both reading the Fire as divine judgement. One makes it 'the law of retribution'; the other says it is unnatural to rejoice at a neighbour's ruin.
